item.title: World Bank Update Outlines AI Productivity Potential and Infrastructure Barriers in Africa
item.description:
World Bank Update Outlines AI Productivity Potential and Infrastructure Barriers in Africa

The World Bank’s October 2026 Africa Economic Update indicates that while artificial intelligence offers promise for the continent’s workers and businesses, it alone cannot bridge the productivity gap. Sub-Saharan Africa’s growth is projected at 4.3% in 2026, up from 4.1% in 2025, but per capita income growth remains low at 1.8%. With over 620 million people expected to enter the labor force by 2050, the report emphasizes creating productive work at scale rather than focusing solely on headline GDP growth.

🔍 Overview

Economic pressures in the region are increasing, making productivity improvements more urgent. The World Bank outlook includes the following fiscal and economic figures:

  • Median Inflation: Projected to rise from 3.7% in 2025 to 5.5% in 2026.
  • Public Debt: Currently stands at approximately 57% of GDP.
  • External Debt Service: Has doubled as a share of revenue, rising from 9% in 2017 to 18% in 2025.

⚙️ Key details

African countries do not need to develop frontier AI systems to benefit from the technology. The immediate opportunity lies in adopting affordable, locally relevant tools that operate on ordinary devices and low-bandwidth conditions. These tools are currently being utilized in agriculture, education, healthcare, logistics, and small businesses. Developer activity is a key indicator of this momentum:

Country GitHub Developer Accounts Growth since 2020
Nigeria 1.8 million Tenfold growth; ranked 11th in EMEA
Kenya 666,020 Follows Nigeria in total accounts
Ghana Not specified Nearly eightfold growth

🧩 How it works

Broad adoption of AI is dependent on prerequisites including devices, electricity, and data access. Current infrastructure and affordability gaps present significant challenges:

  • Infrastructure Access: Only 12% of households in the poorest income quintile have both a phone and a grid connection, compared to 54% among the wealthiest.
  • Internet Affordability: Mobile internet in Sub-Saharan Africa is the least affordable in the world relative to income. A basic data package costs twice the United Nations’ affordability target of 2% of average monthly income.
  • Handset Costs: An entry-level handset costs the poorest fifth of the population about three-quarters of a month’s income.

💡 Why it matters

AI is only effective when users can assess outputs and apply them to real-world problems. To ensure broad benefits, the report suggests that governments and employers prioritize job-specific training for safe and effective AI use. Without intervention, large companies with reliable connectivity may use automation to increase productivity, while informal businesses and rural workers remain excluded. Public procurement, schools, and community health systems could help provide practical AI applications to those unable to purchase them independently. Additionally, clear data-protection laws are essential to mitigate risks such as reproduced biases and the exposure of personal or health information.

#WorldBank #SubSaharanAfrica #DigitalEconomy

Source: AFRICA’S PRODUCTIVITY PROMISE: AI THAT WORKS FOR PEOPLE AND SMALL BUSINESSES - African Leadership Magazine

item.title: World Bank Update Highlights AI Growth and Policy Needs in India
item.description:
World Bank Update Highlights AI Growth and Policy Needs in India

The World Bank released its India Development Update, highlighting AI as a key development opportunity for the country.

📈 Economic Context

  • India’s economy is projected to grow at 7.1% in FY27 supported by robust domestic demand and strong exports, despite global headwinds.
  • It remains one of the fastest‑growing major economies and a key contributor to global growth, according to the World Bank’s latest economic update.
  • The South Asia Economic Update projects regional growth of 6.9% in 2026, keeping South Asia the strongest‑growing region.

🤖 AI Investment and Workforce Trends

  • Private AI investment rose three‑fold, from $1.2 billion in 2024 to $4.1 billion in 2025.
  • Global Capability Centers (GCCs) employed 1.9 million professionals in 2024, increasing to 2.36 million in 2025.
  • India is listed among the top 10 emerging‑market performers on AI readiness.

🛠️ Policy Recommendations

  • The Update calls for cross‑cutting actions to deepen AI‑enabling infrastructure, improve the business environment, broaden AI access, and enhance labor capacity so benefits are broadly shared.
  • Recommended measures include:
    • Strengthening workforce skills.
    • Establishing a more business‑enabling environment.
    • Improving physical and digital infrastructure.
    • Reducing barriers for small firms, fostering local AI innovation, and creating a clear regulatory framework that safeguards data security and privacy.

🌾 Small AI for Development

  • The report stresses that AI should be used as a development tool, not just a technology, to boost productivity and improve public services.
  • Through AgriConnect, the World Bank Group is investing in ‘small AI’: targeted, locally‑adapted tools that ensure gains are accessible and widely shared while supporting workers through the transition.

🌏 Regional Perspective

  • For most of South Asia, the greatest gains lie in adopting AI and adapting it to local conditions, including small AI applications suited to low‑resource settings.
  • “The adoption of AI has the potential to transform South Asia’s development trajectory by boosting labor productivity, expanding export opportunities, and improving public service delivery. But to reap these benefits, governments need to address the foundational gaps that hold back adoption.” – Franziska Ohnsorge, World Bank Group Chief Economist for Asia
  • “India is one of the top 10 leading emerging-market performers on AI readiness**.” – Paul Procee, World Bank Acting Country Director for India

⚠️ External Risks

  • The Update notes elevated external risks, including downside risks from global oil prices, El Niño, and stock‑market corrections that could cause capital‑flow volatility.

#IndiaAI #WorldBank #EconomicDevelopment #ArtificialIntelligence

Source: India’s Growth Intact Despite Global Headwinds; AI Can Create New Opportunities through Policy Actions
